results.whats_broken: VLOOKUP returns #N/A for some rows even though the code visually exists in the price list, most likely because the lookup values don't match exactly (extra spaces or text-vs-number mismatch).
results.why: VLOOKUP with the last argument 0 (or FALSE) demands an exact match. If the code in A2 has a trailing space, a non-breaking space, or is stored as text while the price list stores it as a number (or vice versa), Excel treats them as different values and returns #N/A. That's why it works for some rows and fails for others even though the codes look identical to your eye.
results.what_changed: Wrapped the lookup value in TRIM(CLEAN(...)) to strip stray spaces and invisible characters; if the mismatch is text-vs-number, also convert with VALUE() or TEXT() so both sides use the same data type.

results.whats_broken: The lookup value in D2 doesn't match the values in Orders!B2:B5000 because the order IDs are stored as text in one place and as numbers in the other.
results.why: The green triangles in the corner mean Excel is warning that those cells contain numbers stored as text (or text that looks like a number). XLOOKUP compares values exactly, so the text "12345" is not the same as the number 12345, and it returns #N/A for every row. This is very common with data exported from 1C.
results.what_changed: Converts both the lookup value and the lookup column to text (and removes stray spaces/non-printing characters) so the two sides match. In Excel 365 this works as a normal formula; in older Excel you may need to enter it with Ctrl+Shift+Enter.

results.whats_broken: The formula uses approximate match (TRUE) on a client-name lookup, so it returns the wrong person's price and fails with #N/A when the name sorts before the first entry.
results.why: The last argument TRUE tells Excel to find an approximate match, which only works correctly on sorted numeric ranges. For text like surnames, Excel stops at the last name alphabetically before your search value, so you get a neighbouring client's price, and if the name comes before the first row you get #N/A. Switching to FALSE (exact match) makes Excel find the exact surname or return #N/A only when the name truly isn't in the list.
results.what_changed: Changed the last argument from TRUE to FALSE so the lookup requires an exact surname match instead of an approximate one.

results.whats_broken: The VLOOKUP returns #N/A for every row where the value in column A is not found in the reference list, including blank rows below your data.
results.why: VLOOKUP looks for each value from A2:A inside Ref!A2:B300. When a value is missing there, or when the row is empty, it cannot find a match and shows #N/A. Because ARRAYFORMULA applies the formula to the whole column, those errors appear all the way down under your data.
results.what_changed: Wrapped the lookup in IFERROR to hide #N/A, and added an IF check so blank rows stay blank instead of showing errors.

results.whats_broken: MATCH can't find today's date in the header row, even though it looks like it's there.
results.why: The most likely reason is that the dates in B1:AF1 are not real dates but text that looks like dates (for example, typed as '01.05.2024' or with a leading apostrophe). MATCH compares the actual stored value, and a text 'date' will never equal the real date returned by TODAY(). Another possibility is that the header contains a date-time value (like 01.05.2024 09:00) while TODAY() is just the date at midnight, so they don't match exactly.
results.what_changed: Wraps the header range in DATEVALUE so text dates are converted to real dates before matching. If your Excel version supports it, =XLOOKUP(TODAY(),DATEVALUE($B$1:$AF$1),$B$1:$AF$1) is a cleaner alternative. If the header contains date-times, use =MATCH(TODAY(),INDEX(INT($B$1:$AF$1),0),0) instead.
